Thank you, Chair, and thank you for doing this hearing, and thank you in general for your passion for building schools and for education in the city in general. I also want to thank the School Construction Authority for their work on this proposal and this project and getting to

COMMITTEE ON LANDMARKS, PUBLIC SITINGS, RESILIENCY AND DISPOSITIONS 6 see firsthand the amount of work and the willingness for feedback that they consider on a proposal like this has caused me to develop a whole new appreciation and respect for the School Construction Authority. Now, when a project like this comes before us, the question is not whether change is coming to a neighborhood. The question is what kind of change we're choosing. And over the past several months I've made it a priority to visit every public school in my District. I've walked the hallways, spoken with principals, teachers, and parents, and seen firsthand the challenges that they're dealing with. And what I saw consistently in my District was overcrowding, classrooms stretched to capacity, spaces being used in ways that they were never intended to be used. And that's before fully accounting for the new class size mandate, which is going to require even more spaces in the years ahead. So, my thinking on this project and on this location has evolved because when you see it up close, when you hear it directly from the people on the front lines, it becomes very clear that we need more school seats in Staten Island. And this proposal would bring

COMMITTEE ON LANDMARKS, PUBLIC SITINGS, RESILIENCY AND DISPOSITIONS 7 more than 750 new seats to our borough and help relieve pressure on nearby schools like PS-32, PS-42, PS-53, IS-24. Just as importantly, it would provide families with a modern state-of-the-art educational facility that can serve this community for generations. But I also think it's important to speak honestly about the broader context that we're operating in. In today's City of Yes environment, vacant land like this is not going to remain vacant. If this site isn't used for a school, it's going to be used for something else. Under current zoning, it could support a significant amount of residential development. And in other parts of the city, we're seeing proposals for uses like this become battery energy storage facilities in close proximities to homes. So, while some may wish this land could remain untouched, the realistic alternative is likely something far more intensive and far more detrimental to a neighborhood than a school. So, at the same time, I want to acknowledge the residents who live on and around East Reading Avenue. I've met with them, I've listened to them, I've watched as several of them have stormed out of my office as I explained that I was going to be supporting this proposal. And

COMMITTEE ON LANDMARKS, PUBLIC SITINGS, RESILIENCY AND DISPOSITIONS 8 I've heard their concerns about traffic, about parking, and their concerns about safety, and those are real and they deserve to be addressed. This vote today is about site selection. It's not the final word on design. The design phase is where many of these issues will be worked out, and I strongly encourage the School Construction Authority to continue engaging with the community in a meaningful way as those plans are developed, because I can tell you in my conversations with people that live here, it's not simply a not in my backyard or not in my front yard situation. These are folks with legitimate concerns about parking, about traffic, about flooding, about ice. And I hope that once this project is designed, some of those concerns are addressed. If we take the time to get the details right, this school can become something the neighborhood embraces rather than something that it feels imposed upon it. Because schools, when done right, aren't disruptions, they're anchors. They're places where communities come together and where the next generation is shaped. And yes, if we do this right, the biggest concern on East Reading Avenue one day might just be finding a parking spot for a school

COMMITTEE ON LANDMARKS, PUBLIC SITINGS, RESILIENCY AND DISPOSITIONS 9 play or a graduation ceremony, and that's a problem most neighborhoods would be proud to have, especially in this environment. For all those reasons, I support moving forward with this project, and I look forward to working with SCA and the community to make sure it's done the right way. Thank you.

Well said. Appearing today from SCA on this proposal is Joseph Jean-Baptiste and Andrea Bender. Those wishing to testify remotely must register online by visiting Council website at council.nyc.gov/landuse. Panelists, please ensure your microphones are on. Counsel, would you please administer the affirmation? Panelists, would you please raise your right hand and state your name for the record?
Andrea Bender.
Joseph Jean-Baptiste.

Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth

COMMITTEE ON LANDMARKS, PUBLIC SITINGS, RESILIENCY AND DISPOSITIONS 10 in your testimony before this Subcommittee and in answer to all Council Member questions?
Yes.
Yes.
Thank you, panelists. You may begin.

Good morning, Chair Marte and Council Member Morano. My name is Andrea Bender. I am Vice President of External Affairs at the New York City School Construction Authority. I am joined by Joseph Jean-Baptiste, our Senior Management Specialist at the SCA. We are pleased to present --actually, I'm sorry, next slide, please. We are pleased to present a proposed new approximately 754-seat PS/IS at East Reading Avenue between Armstrong Avenue and Abingdon Avenues in the Great Kills neighborhood of Staten Island. This proposed project, as we all know, is in Council Member Frank Morano's District, and we thank him wholeheartedly for his partnership and support on this project. Next slide, please. Pursuant to Section 1731 of the New York State Public Authorities Law, the New York City School Construction Authority has undertaken the site

COMMITTEE ON LANDMARKS, PUBLIC SITINGS, RESILIENCY AND DISPOSITIONS 11 selection process for a new approximately 754-seat primary intermediate school facility located at Abingdon Avenue between East Perkiomen Avenue and East Reading Avenue Block 5474, Lots 12 through 29 in the Borough of Staten Island. The site is approximately 96,000 square feet, 2.2 acres, and is located within Staten Island Community Board Number 3 and Community Education Council District Number 31. The purpose of the proposed project is to provide additional long-term capacity to relieve overcrowding in School District 31. The five-year capital plan for Fiscal Years 2025 to 2029 allocates capital funding to address existing overcrowding and forecasted changes in student enrollment and to support New York City Public Schools' policies regarding class size reduction. During the 2023-2024 school year, Community Education Council 31's elementary schools collectively operated at 112 percent of their targeted capacity, as Council Member Murano clearly noticed on his school tours. Next slide, please. So, here we have an aerial view of the site. As you can see, it's bounded by Abingdon and Armstrong, the easement for the unbuilt East

COMMITTEE ON LANDMARKS, PUBLIC SITINGS, RESILIENCY AND DISPOSITIONS 12 Perkiomen and East Reading Avenues. Next slide, please. The notice of filing of the site plan was published in AM New York and The City Record on May 8th, 2025, at which time CEC 31, Staten Island Community Board 3, and the City Planning Commission were notified of the proposed site plan. Community Board 3 held a public hearing on May 14th, 2025, and the Community Education Council held a public hearing on June 9th, 2025. All public comments received on the site were considered as part of the site plan. Next slide, please. So, here we have some photos of the current conditions on the site, view of the project site facing northwest from the intersection of East Reading and Abingdon, a view of the project site and the unpaved portion of the easement for East Perkiomen facing east along the paved portion, sort of the backside of the site. Next slide, please. Some more photos of the site in its current condition, view facing north along Abingdon. The project site including the portion separated from the street with a guardrail is visible on the right, and then the opposite picture is the view facing east

COMMITTEE ON LANDMARKS, PUBLIC SITINGS, RESILIENCY AND DISPOSITIONS 13 along East Reading Avenue, one- and two-family homes across the street, and the project site is visible to the left. Next slide, please. One last view of the project area, the view facing northwest along East Reading Avenue, showing the border between the project site and the adjacent homes on Block 5474. Next slide, please. The SCA affirms the site plan pursuant to Section 1731 of the New York Public Authorities Law. In accordance with Section 1732 of the Public Authorities Law, the SCA submitted the proposed site plan to the Mayor and City Council by letter dated February 23rd, 2026. Should SCA receive approval to acquire the property, a new PS/IS will be constructed and is anticipated to open in 2031. The proposed school will include approximately 31 classrooms for pre-K through 8th grade, two special education classrooms, 10 District 75 classrooms, a speech resource room, a reading resource room, a music room, an art room, kitchen-cafeteria, library, gymnatorium, guidance and medical suites, as well as general administrative and support spaces. The site plan also includes two at-grade play yards totaling approximately 23,700 square feet. Next slide, please.

COMMITTEE ON LANDMARKS, PUBLIC SITINGS, RESILIENCY AND DISPOSITIONS 14 We look forward to the Subcommittee's favorable consideration of the proposed plan and would be happy to answer any questions that you might have. Thank you so much.
Thank you. Council Member Morano, do you have any questions?

Sure. I'll ask a couple brief ones. Thank you again for all your work on this, and thank you for being so willing to address all of my substantial number of questions throughout this process. One question that did come up from a couple of neighborhood residents, and I'll ask on their behalf, is a lot of them I think have come to understand that a school is a positive thing for a community and certainly better than a lot of the other alternatives. But some people raised, well, does it have to be such a large school, does it have to be 760 students and 98 faculty members? And they're concerned with the traffic and parking implications of that. Can you talk about how that size was developed and if there's any realistic prospect for making it a smaller school?

COMMITTEE ON LANDMARKS, PUBLIC SITINGS, RESILIENCY AND DISPOSITIONS 15

Sure. So, based on the size of the property and the need in the surrounding community we like to, where we can, maximize our development to meet the needs of the school district in question. It is important to note that we did analyze in our SEQR analysis the impacts on traffic, parking, and other community, resources and, along with the mitigations that our SEQR analysis identified for some signalization on some area streets, there was no impact found to traffic flow in the neighborhood and there appears to be, based on my own experience and based on the SEQR findings, substantial parking able to accommodate the traffic generated by students and staff driving to the site. The impact on parking was very minimal and only reduced the available parking spaces by approximately 6 percent, still leaving a very significant number of spaces available. So, I understand the community's concerns very much. This is a common concern that we get across the city. One of the things that often takes a minute is once the school opens and traffic patterns sort of stabilize, the impact tends to be much less than people anticipate just based on their own experience or their own anecdotal information,

COMMITTEE ON LANDMARKS, PUBLIC SITINGS, RESILIENCY AND DISPOSITIONS 16 but our SEQR analysis does show that there would be no impact to traffic and no impact to parking. And our goal here is really to maximize the development that's needed to meet the needs of the school district.

I asked you this privately, but I'll go ahead and ask it publicly for everybody's sake. Will SCA commit to holding at least one public meeting with residents during the design phase so that they can weigh in on traffic, parking, and the layout?
Certainly.

In terms of the entrance location, there was one design that was floating around somewhere that a couple people were, you know, emailing me over the last couple days. Has a final decision been made on where the primary entrance will be, and will the community have input on that before it's finalized?

So, when we analyze a site for a potential school, we are looking to make sure before we purchase a property, we are looking to make sure that the program that we would like can actually fit on that property, and we have to work with DOT

COMMITTEE ON LANDMARKS, PUBLIC SITINGS, RESILIENCY AND DISPOSITIONS 17 and other regulatory agencies to develop some kinds of assumptions to analyze traffic, parking, other impacts. So, we have a conceptual plan that is in our SEQR analysis that shows an entrance for the purposes of study. That is not the basis of design. We have not started design. We do not start design until we close on the property. And so, when we enter into design, the architect team will look at the street grid in the area and they will look at proposed openings that make the most sense for ease of drop-off and pickup for buses, for families. They will certainly look at how that will affect the community. I'm certainly happy to take the community's input on where the proposed entrance location that might work best for them. I'm certainly happy to relay that. What I would say is that for safety and operational reasons, we would want to reserve final decisions on those considerations to the architects.
Sure.

Again, absolutely happy to take those considerations from the community back to the design team.

COMMITTEE ON LANDMARKS, PUBLIC SITINGS, RESILIENCY AND DISPOSITIONS 18

You mentioned the SEQR analysis. Can you confirm for the record that the Phase 1 and Phase 2 environmental reviews didn't identify any contamination that would prevent a school from being built safely on the site? I know there was some concerns about soil when people first heard about this project.

Yes. The SEQR analysis identifies that the subject property has not been meaningfully developed since at least the 1920s and consists largely of native soils and historic fill, which is consistent with sites that we see pretty much everywhere in the city.
Lastly, can you briefly explain to folks why this site was selected over other potential locations, including publicly owned sites?

Sure. So, at this time in this area, to our knowledge, there are not other sites that are as large and also available for acquisition at this time. That is why this site was selected. I am not aware of publicly owned sites in the immediate vicinity of this site. I'm aware of some publicly owned sites sort of elsewhere on Staten

COMMITTEE ON LANDMARKS, PUBLIC SITINGS, RESILIENCY AND DISPOSITIONS 19 Island. We love developing on publicly owned sites where we can because it frees us from spending millions of dollars to acquire property. So, if you have publicly owned sites that you'd like us to look at, please let us know. That goes for any Council Member. But that's why this site.
Thanks very much.
Yeah.
I would like to recognize Council Member Thomas-Henry and Council Member Avilés. Do any other council members have any questions? All right. Thank you. This applicant panel is now excused.
Thank you so much.
Appreciate it. Thank you.
Counsel, are there any members of the public who wish to testify on this item?
No, there are not.

Okay.

And if you're here with us in person, please see one of the Sergeant-at-Arms arms to first fill out a speaker card. All right. There being no other members of the public who wish to testify regarding the public SCA school site, the items are now laid over. Thank you. That concludes today's business, and I'd like to thank the members of the public, my Colleagues, Subcommittee Counsel, Land Use Staff, and the Sergeant-at-Arms for your participation today. This meeting is now adjourned. Thank you. [GAVEL]

Testing one, two, one two. Today’s March 18, 2026. Today’s Committee hearing is on Cultural Affairs, Libraries and International Intergroup Relations being recorded in HR 1 by Keith Polite.

Good morning and welcome to the New York City Council Committee on Cultural Affairs, Libraries, and International Intergroup. Please do not approach the dais at any time during this hearing. Please place your phone on silent mode. Chair, thank you for your cooperation. We are ready to begin.

Thank you Sergeants. [GAVEL] Good morning and thank you to everyone joining us today for the Committee on Cultural Affairs, Libraries, and International Relations Fiscal Year 2027 Preliminary Budget Hearing. I would like to welcome the representatives from the three public library systems, members of the public and my colleagues and the Council. Our public libraries are among the most trusted and widely used institutions in our city. As I convene my first budget hearing as Chair of this Committee, I must emphasize the critical role libraries play for New

Yorkers. Far beyond housing books, libraries are vital community hubs providing job training, tech access and educational support. Serving as a true lifeline for residents citywide. However, year after year, the Council finds itself returning to the same conversation during the budget process. At the preliminary budget stage, the full level of funding libraries require is often absent. Creating uncertainty for the systems and the communities that rely on them. I was very disappointed to see that the preliminary plan did not include the one time funding of $30.7 million added at adoption of the Fiscal 2026 budget. I would have liked to see this funding baselined. This recurring pattern forces the Council to step in each year to restore or add funding simply to maintain existing services. Rather than allowing the library systems to plan with stability and focus on expanding programs and resources for New Yorkers. This cycle makes it extremely difficult for library systems to plan ahead. Without stable funding at the start of the Fiscal Year, libraries face uncertainty in staffing, programming, and long term service planning. Our library system should not

have to operate with this level of uncertainty when they are providing essential services to millions of New Yorkers. Today, we will also be discussing the significant challenges libraries face in completing capital projects in a timely manner. Across the city, many library branches require renovations, accessibility upgrades and critical infrastructure improvements. Yet, these projects often take many years to move from planning to completion. Lengthy timelines, complex approval and procurement processes and rising construction costs can delay projects well beyond their original schedules, leaving communities waiting far too long for modernized and fully accessible library spaces. If we want libraries to continue serving as the cornerstone institutions they are, we must ensure they have both the operating support and capital resources necessary to maintain and modernize their facilities. I look forward to hearing from the leadership of our three library systems today about how the preliminary budget impacts their ability to serve New

Yorkers and how we can work together to provide the stability and investments they need. Before we begin, I would like to acknowledge my colleagues who are present. We have Finance Chair Lee, Council Member Maloney, Council Member Louis and Council Member Hudson. I would also like to thank the Finance Staff, Carolina and Aliya for their work on this hearing. As well as Committee Staff Alejandro and Regina for their support. Finally, I would also like to thank my staff Priyanka(SP?) and Shakee (SP?). I would also like to remind everyone from the public who wishes to testify in person today that you must fill out an appearance card, which is located on the desks of the Sergeant at Arms at the back of the room. Please fill out the slip even if you have already registered to testify in advance. When you are called, please limit your testimony to two minutes, whether you are testifying in person or in Zoom. I am also going to ask my colleagues to limit their questions and commits to five minutes. Okay, so I will now invite the libraries to testify.

Good morning. Can you hear me? Good morning, I’m Tony Marx and I’m the President of the New York Public Library and it’s an honor and pleasure to be with you here this morning. I want to thank - start by thanking City Council Speaker Menin as well as Deputy Speaker and Committee Chair Dr. Nantasha Williams. Congratulations on your new post and thank you for those comments. I couldn’t have said it better myself. And also, thanks to the whole Committee and its staff for the opportunity to testify today on the Mayor’s Fiscal 2027 Preliminary Budget. Over the last several years, the library has repeatedly faced significant cuts to its operating budget. Each year starts with a setback that we spend the subsequent months spending resources to reverse. Last year, uncharacteristically started off better. We were held harmless, even allocated an additional $2 million to expand Sunday services by the City Council. But we still had to campaign to be baselined and we weren't, even though our peer institutions in the city were. This is still the budget dance, as the Chair has referred to it. It is laborious, it is costly, and it deverts valuable

staff and other resources from our vital offerings in the fight to keep even. This near annual exercise has left us with mostly flat budgets for several years amid rising costs. Naturally, we were thrilled to learn of the then mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani’s promise to literally end the budget dance with consistent baselined funding of 0.5 percent of the city’s budget. His mayoralty represents, in his own words, a new era for both the city at large and for libraries in particular. We can together turn the page on the past with an administration that understands that libraries are an integral part to a more affordable New York. We’ve already had some great interactions with the Administration. We lent the Mayor the Quran that he was sworn in on. We hosted him for the city’s annual interfaith breakfast. We’ve discussed future partnership and shared priorities on digital equity and literacy, as well as on collocations on affordable housing above new libraries. This positive relationship has extended to encouraging discussions about the city budget. We are grateful for his baselining of the City Council’s

$2 million in the Mayor’s Preliminary Budget to maintain the added Sunday service locations from last year. The Administration has also been receptive to the impacts of the proposed savings targets for the current and forthcoming year as well as reductions in the FY27 Preliminary Budget on our offerings. We are aware of the $5 billion deficit that the city faces and its ongoing conversations with the state but we are heartened by the Administration's acknowledgement of the outsized returns on investments that libraries provide to all, to all New Yorkers. It is still early in the process and we are confident that the Mayor’s intent on delivering on both of his campaign promises. Baselined funding at 0.5 percent stands to transform library services into a resource with a credible presence that New Yorkers never have to question or wonder about. We can fortify our services, which means more hours and days of operations with more of our great staff. And more hours and days of operations in staff, means that the branches can provide college and career advice for graduating high school seniors. Our teen centers can do their work for young adults to socialize with their peers. We could provide an

open place for kids to drop in for afterschool tutoring. A trusted place for New Yorkers and we are the most trusted place for all New Yorkers in every neighborhood for all income levels, for instance to help filing their taxes. The demand for these and other services is very real. Last year, our afterschool attendance was over 68,000 students. We’ll surpass that this year as a quarter over quarter growth already shows a 25 percent increase. A recent career resources fair for teens hosted 1,600 attendees with over 40 businesses and other organizations. The FY26 PMMR shows a steady increase of program attendance, library card holders, computer and wireless sessions from FY23 through FY25. And in January, the New York Times survey of 35,000 New Yorkers showed more funding for libraries to be their very top choice. We can also address our unmet needs of $24 million, a product of operating on this flat budget along with the rising costs of collections, staff wages and IT. We hope this commitment to libraries will also include as the Chair mentioned, our capital agenda. Our services are of little value, if they do not

happen in places that feel safe, welcoming and respectful of New Yorkers rights to knowledge and opportunity, let alone if those spaces are not open. The libraries currently have $1.2 billion in unmet capital needs, $485 million of that is just at the New York Public Library. This is because most of our buildings are aging. They’re small structures, beloved but small and aging. The city’s capital process also often results in costly budget shortfalls and significant delays, also as the Chair has mentioned. Mayor Mamdani’s commitment to excellence in government makes us hopeful that we can finally address these systemic issues with reform in the near future. We look forward to partnership in the meantime or short term fixes. One example would be a transformative investment in the ten year capital plan. Much has happened in 2016 with $100 million that allowed us to fully renovate five century old Carnegie libraries in high needs neighborhoods in the Bronx, Manhattan and Staten Island. Another, as I mentioned, is the collocation projects, which allow us to take advantage of the air above old libraries, build new

libraries with affordable housing above, as we did in the first instance in Inwood. And we can experiment with other ways to streamline our design construction and to be - that are already being employed at the new library at West Chester Square. The Council has always been and continues to be a most reliable ally. Every time the library has faced significant cuts in the past, it was the library council who took up our cause and joined in the fight for restoration, including the additional funding in FY26. Speaker Menin, a long time friend of the library, has confirmed that this continues to be the case. Recently, when she stated that libraries are New Yorkers' most trusted institutions. As in deed they are. We know and recognize, this is a challenging time for this city financially. We understand that these challenges were inherited, as well as the intergovernmental dynamics at play. We also know that it is still early. The City Council is as always with us and we have a new Mayor who appreciates the libraries as an unparalleled crucial public good within the lives of New Yorkers.

We are living with a different Mayor and a different City Council in a different day. Everyone is paying attention. Everyone is committed to investing in the libraries, so that we can continue to invest in all New Yorkers. I look forward to retiring my dancing shoes. Thank you Madam Chair and all colleagues.

Who knew Tony had dancing shoes? Good morning, sorry, excuse me. I am Linda Johnson, President and CEO of Brooklyn Public Library. Thank you to Speaker Menin and to our new Chair, Deputy Speaker Dr. Williams, as well as Finance Chair Lee, the Members of the Committee and the entire City Council for your steadfast support of New York City’s libraries. Your commitment to libraries makes it possible for us to deliver the programs, services and resources New Yorkers count on every day. I would also like to recognize and thank the library workers who make this work possible, including our partners at DC37 and Brooklyn Public Libraries local 1482. Library staff are the frontline of service for millions of New Yorkers and their dedication is the reason libraries are among

the most beloved and trusted institutions in our cities. Forgive me, some of my testimony is going to repeat what my colleague from the New York Public Library has just stated but I think it bears repeating. Uhm, for years, libraries have endured an annual ritual no city organization should face, with or without dancing shoes. Funded, allocated as a temporary measure, only to vanish from the Preliminary Budget requiring us to return here to make the case all over again. That pattern has had real consequences for staff morale, for our ability to plan, and for the New Yorkers who depend upon us. The Mayor’s Preliminary Budget takes a step toward ending the budget dance both baselining the $2 million of the $32.7 million increase, the Council secured in Fiscal 2026 and pledging to work with us to maintain service labels. We have had many productive conversations with the Administration and they have been transparent about the city’s budget pressures. They also understand what the Council has long championed, that libraries are central to the city’s affordability agenda and

must be a priority. We are hopeful and we will continue that conversation. I often say that libraries are the modern day town square. A trusted space to access information, to connect with neighbors and discuss critical questions of their time. We welcome New Yorkers from every neighborhood and every walk of life and we ask for nothing in return. Your investment last year marked an important step forward for libraries. At Brooklyn Public Library, your support enabled us to open Bay Ridge and Bedford Libraries on Sundays, hire additional staff, expand our collections, and address emergency building maintenance. New Yorkers noticed this investment. Brooklyn Public Library 62 locations received over 6 million visits last year. Patrons checked out nearly 10 million items, including books and digital materials, as well as items from our library of things, borrowing board games, musical instruments, power tools for home projects, telescopes, vinyl records, museum passes, and even art work. Overall, our circulation is 7 percent higher year to date over the past fiscal year. Our Culture Pass program is set to have its strongest year since launching in 2018 with over

75,000 passes checked out between July 2025 and February 2026. Library workers hosted more than 80,000 free programs in Brooklyn alone, including our Text Help programs, which helped over 1,500 Brooklyn residents collectively save more than $2 million on their taxes last year. Attendance at our First Five Years program is up 13 percent, putting us on pace for our busiest year of Early Childhood programming since the pandemic. Driven in large part by programs funded through the City Council’s First Readers Initiative. The Preliminary Budget moves libraries in the right direction and I’m optimistic that the adopted budget on the Council’s fiscal will build on the Council’s Fiscal 2026 investment and put us on a path toward greater stability. The challenges are real. The federal prohibition on passport services at nonprofit library alone, costs Brooklyn Public Library nearly $1 million annually. Our participation in the city’s cost savings exercise and personnel materials and maintenance costs continue to climb. These are real pressures but they also underscore the importance of

investing in what libraries can deliver for New Yorkers. We welcome the conversation about what one half of one percent of the city budget would unlock for New York City’s libraries. In Brooklyn, this means hiring specialists dedicated to every age group across our branches. So, children, teens, adults and older adults all have access to the programs and resources they need no matter where they live. It means expanding service hours so working families can visit after work and students have more time to study. It means responding quickly to urgent building needs rather than waiting years for a capital project to wind through the pipeline, keeping our doors open and our libraries safe. It is the level of service New Yorkers deserve and as a January New York Times poll showed, proudly demand. You have Brooklyn Public Library’s capital needs spelled out in front of you. In the interest of time, I won't read all of this but I do want to note the need facing Brooklyn’s Library is significant, as is the progress we’ve made together. Council Member support for our projects, as well as the Council’s extraordinary capital allocation

last year, have been essential. To this end, I am requesting the City Council alongside the Brooklyn delegation once again, allocate $10 million in discretionary capital funding for systemwide repairs, project shortfalls and essential upgrades at Brooklyn’s branches. We are also submitting a capital request to the Administration for a transformational investment, $150 million for each library system to comprehensively upgrade more than a dozen libraries across the city. It’s time to move beyond using expense money for bandages and invest in top to bottom renovations that save time and money, reduce interruptions and create inspiring state of the art libraries built to last. Thank you for the opportunity to discuss the preliminary budget. The Council has been a longstanding champion of libraries and we are all grateful for your leadership. I’d like to end by sharing a very brief poem by Live Lusk, a patron of our Marcy Library. It’s titled, ‘My Library is Loud.’ With children giggling over picture books with faces that look like theirs. With hushed conversations a man is rehearsing for his job interview on Friday. The first one since he was

incarcerated. With keyboards clacking, a young man is watching a video on how to create the best transit city in Minecraft. With printers spitting fresh copies of a missing cat poster, a father and daughter will spend the afternoon placing them around the neighborhood only for mittens to appear at 6 p.m. sharp for dinner. A woman is soothing herself with rhythmic chance because the library is the only place she feels safe to do so. My library is loud and I feel joy. Your continued support ensures our libraries remain vibrant and loud with activity and future generations who will know this joy. Thank you.

Good morning. Good morning. There we go. To Chair, Deputy Speaker, Dr. Nantasha Williams, congratulations. It’s a pleasure to greet you. To Finance Chair Linda Lee, it’s a pleasure to see you as well. To our Queens representative as well, Council Member Sandra Ung, a pleasure. To the members of this esteemed Committee and to our ongoing supporter Speaker Julie Menin, thank you for all of your support. I am Dennis Walcott, President and CEO of the Queens Public Library. It is a pleasure to be here

with you today. To our great team members who are here from the Queens Public Library, to our union President John Hislop(SP?) who is sitting somewhere in the audience as well. Thank you for your partnership and ongoing support. We are here to talk about our great libraries. It is 10:03 and I know at Queens, people are streaming through the doors coming to receive our services and they’re entering looking for hope, opportunity, information, services and just to become better people and we are very, very thankful for all the great staff who are working, providing the services there. I have submitted written testimony; however, I will forgo reading it to emphasize a few key points.
